comparison: Sec 5.3 (RQ3), Table 4: raw functions flagged by GPT matching before vs after static confirmation, on Web3Bugs
model_config: Same run of the same pipeline, so the same model in both arms. Sec 4.5 names GPT-3.5-turbo; Sec 5.3 names no model.
dataset_metric: Web3Bugs only; counts of raw (unmerged) candidate functions, 647 before vs 221 after
budget_control: not applicable; GPT input is identical in both arms (the arms are two stages of one run)
arm_a: GPT-matched candidate functions (pure GPT-based matching output)
arm_b: Same candidates after the static-analysis (dataflow) confirmation stage filters them
other_changes: Adds or removes the static confirmation stage, a symbolic post-filter. GPT's input representation does not change. It is a before/after measurement within one run, not a separately run ablation.
delta: "Static confirmation effectively filtered out 65.84% of the false positive cases in the Web3Bugs dataset" (647 -> 221 raw functions); "only 3 ground-truth cases were initially matched by GPT but later excluded by static analysis"
rationale: RQ3 examines "how static confirmation reduces false positives generated by pure GPT-based matching." The varied factor is a symbolic confirmation stage, not the representation supplied to GPT. The paper contains no input-representation ablation: its only other comparisons use David et al.'s published GPT-only figures and a GPT-4 model swap. The 426 filtered raw functions include a few ground-truth cases, so 65.84% is a reduction in raw functions, not a clean false-positive count.

comparison: RQ4 ablation, Table 6: full SCALE vs Without SER (the cited one) and vs Without SCTC. Table 3 is a cross-model comparison.
model_config: Fine-tuned UniXcoder backbone (lr 2e-5, 8 cross-attention heads, batch 32). Without SER removes the cross-attention fusion module. Without SCTC keeps the architecture.
dataset_metric: FFMPeg+Qemu, Reveal, SVulD (8:1:1 splits); F1 (also Acc/P/R)
budget_control: not reported (no max sequence length, truncation, or token budget stated)
arm_a: Full SCALE: source code plus the rule-structured comment tree (SCT), fused by cross-attention (SER)
arm_b: Without SER: "structured natural language comments as input without the source code" (no code, no fusion). Without SCTC: the plain comment tree instead of the rule-structured SCT, with SER kept.
other_changes: Without SER removes an architectural module (cross-attention fusion of the code and SCT representations) and drops source code from the input. Every arm is separately fine-tuned.
delta: Removing SER drops F1 by "1.31, 3.61, and 3.56" points (Table 6: 65.11->63.80, 62.85->59.24, 26.94->23.38). Removing SCTC drops F1 by "1.29, 2.59, and 2.04" points; the paper's SVulD figure does not match Table 6 (26.94-24.99=1.95).
rationale: The cited ablation removes SER, which "fuse[s] the representation of source code and structured natural language comment through Cross-Attention," an architectural component, and also removes source code from the input. The cleanest comparison is Without SCTC (plain comment tree vs SCT, same architecture), but its input lengths are not reported, so at best it is R-unmatched-budget, not R-strict. Table 3 and RQ2 swap backbones, so they are not isolated.

comparison: Table I / Fig. 4: repair with no context (15%) vs full context-aware prompt tuning (63%)
model_config: GitHub Copilot in all conditions. Copilot version, sampling settings, and session handling are not reported.
dataset_metric: Custom set of 156 buffer-overflow C snippets; manually judged repair success rate
arm_a: Single repair prompt with the snippet only ("fix any vulnerability")
arm_b: Staged waterfall. A detection question comes first, and the author supplies the correct answer if detection is wrong. Each failed repair moves to the next stage, which adds disclosure, then CWE detail, then code-context cues (buffer identification, bound selection, range precision, placement).
other_changes: Prompt paradigm differs. The 63% arm is multi-turn and interactive, with human correction of wrong detections and retries across stages. The 15% arm is a single prompt. The number of iterations per snippet is not reported.
delta: 15% (24/156) no-context repair vs 63% after full context-aware prompt tuning (">4x")
rationale: The 63% figure comes from a multi-stage process in which, "if detection is wrong, the author supplies the correct answer," and failed repairs escalate to the next stage. Interaction paradigm, human feedback, and retries therefore vary along with context. The cleaner single-prompt comparison, no context 15% vs CWE detail 31% (48/156), has the same model and only added context, but prompt length is not reported, so it would be R-unmatched-budget, not R-strict. The paper's text and Table I are also inconsistent on the disclosure and CWE percentages.

comparison: Table 6 / Appendix C ablations: RepoAudit vs RepoAudit-NoAbs and vs RepoAudit-NoVal
model_config: Same agent and LLM in every arm. The ablation section names no model; Sec 4 says Claude 3.5 Sonnet powers RepoAudit.
dataset_metric: 15-project C/C++ benchmark (NPD, MLK, UAF); TP/FP counts and precision
budget_control: not reported (no token or cost figures for NoAbs or NoVal; cost is reported only for NoCache, Table 7)
arm_a: Full RepoAudit: function code plus a three-step hint prompt (pointer handling, abstraction, path exploration), followed by the validator
arm_b: NoAbs: the same code, minus the second (abstraction) step of the prompt template. NoVal: the same explorer prompts, with the validator (parser-based control-flow alignment and LLM path-feasibility check) removed.
other_changes: NoVal removes a verification stage. NoAbs removes a reasoning instruction from the prompt, not a supplied representation: the code shown to the LLM is the same and the LLM performs the abstraction itself.
delta: Precision 78.43% (40TP/11FP) full vs 40.38% (21TP/31FP) NoAbs vs 40TP/38FP NoVal (51.28% computed from the totals; the paper does not state it)
rationale: NoVal "removes the validation of the data-flow facts discovered by the explorer and also skips examining the bug reports," a verification-stage removal. NoAbs "skips the program abstraction, i.e., removing the second step in the prompt template," a change to the prompting procedure that leaves the supplied code representation unchanged. Neither arm isolates representation. The paper's NoVal text says FPs "increase to 31," but Table 6 and its +245.45% give 38.

source_checked: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.11561v1 (no HTML version available; v1 is the only version)
comparison: Table 1 / Sec 4.2: GPT-4o baseline (11-12-14) vs Short + CVE Hints + Manual (18-14-17). The cleaner within-template comparison is Short (13-13-13) vs Short + CVE Hints + Manual.
model_config: GPT-4o in all arms, temperature 0.01, 3 generations per prompt
dataset_metric: Vul4J, 42 vulnerabilities; successful repairs per run (unit-test validated, with limited manual checks)
budget_control: not controlled or reported. The Short prompt was designed for "minimizing token usage," but token counts are not given, and the added-context arms add CVE guidelines plus manual repository context on top of Short.
arm_a: GPT-4o baseline: the original prompt from the prior study (parent class header, data members, vulnerable method). Cleaner alternative: Short, a condensed system prompt with refined code input.
arm_b: Short + CVE Hints + Manual: Short prompt plus GPT-generated CVE-based repair guidelines plus "manually collected repository and issue-related information"
other_changes: Against the GPT-4o baseline, the instruction template and code-input preparation also differ (Sec 3.2: added method headers, imports, pruned data members, new system prompt). Against Short there are no other changes; the paradigm stays zero-shot single prompt.
delta: 18-14-17 vs 11-12-14 (baseline) and vs 13-13-13 (Short), successful repairs out of 42 per run; absolute counts, no pp or relative figure stated
rationale: Model, temperature, and dataset are fixed, and the arms differ only in prompt content. The added-context arm appends CVE guidelines and "manually collected repository and issue-related information," and its length is not reported, so representation is confounded with context amount. The cited baseline arm also uses a different instruction template, so Short vs Short + CVE Hints + Manual is the cleaner comparison. Neither is R-strict. Short + Manual alone (9-13-10) scored below Short.

source_checked: https://arxiv.org/html/2508.13092 (latest; abs page lists v3, 21 Aug 2025)
comparison: Table 2: LLM-only vs LLM+Knowledge vs VerilogLAVD, per backbone
model_config: The same backbones (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3) are used across arms, 5 runs each, Pass@5. The LLM's role differs: judge in the baselines, rule generator in VerilogLAVD.
dataset_metric: 77 Verilog designs (59 positive / 18 negative, 12 CWEs); precision/recall/F1
arm_a: LLM+Knowledge: Verilog code, a brief CWE description, and detailed MITRE CWE information; the LLM judges directly
arm_b: VerilogLAVD: the LLM generates VeriPG traversal rules, checked by a rule-validation tool with feedback, and a rule executor traverses the VeriPG graph (AST+CFG+DDG) to detect
other_changes: Adds a symbolic rule executor (detection is done by graph traversal, not by the LLM) and a rule-validation feedback loop. The LLM's task changes from classification to rule generation.
delta: F1 0.57 vs 0.25 (GPT-4o) and 0.50 vs 0.34 (DeepSeek-V3), absolute F1. Abstract and conclusion inconsistent: abstract F1 0.54 and gain 0.27 vs conclusion 0.25.
rationale: The paper states that "LLMs are responsible for generating VeriPG traversal-based detection rules," which "avoids direct structural reasoning": a rule executor performs detection over the graph, and a validator feeds back during generation. The arms therefore differ by symbolic execution and verification components, not by the representation given to the same LLM judgment. There is no arm in which the LLM judges with the graph as input.

comparison: RQ3 ablation, Table IV (CodeQL rulesets R1-R7). The cited RQ1 comparison is CodeQL default vs SemTaint.
model_config: Detection is done by CodeQL in every arm. LLM agents (GPT-5 for Source/Sink and Flow Summary, GPT-5-mini for CallGraph) only produce specifications. The record's "GPT-4 vs GPT-4-mini" is incorrect.
dataset_metric: Known Vulnerability Dataset, 162 test instances; recall and first-detecting ruleset
budget_control: not applicable (the varied input feeds a static analyzer, not an LLM prompt)
arm_a: R3: SemTaint custom sources/sinks with CodeQL's base call graph
arm_b: R4/R6: custom or combined sources/sinks with the LLM-repaired (enhanced) call graph. R1: CodeQL defaults with no LLM.
other_changes: The arms toggle LLM-derived analyzer configuration (spec set, call-graph repair by the CallGraph Agent, barriers) inside a symbolic taint engine. RQ1's baseline has no LLM at all.
delta: RQ1: "SemTaint identified the vulnerability in 106 instances, which represents a recall of 65.43%" vs CodeQL default 0%. RQ3: 81/106 (76.42%) "Just source/sink" vs 25/106 (23.58%) "Needed call graph".
rationale: The paper says "the resulting taint specification is then provided to a SAST tool, which performs vulnerability analysis." RQ3 therefore adds or removes LLM-generated pipeline components (call-graph repair) inside CodeQL, not the representation an LLM reasons over. RQ1 compares against a non-LLM tool and is not isolated. The combined-dataset split (73.0/27.0) should not be mixed with the testing-only split (76.4/23.6).

comparison: Table 6 (C): Code-Only (CO) vs Code+Callees (CC) vs Code+Callers (CK), per model
model_config: Same model per comparison (GPT-4.1 Mini, GPT-5 Mini, Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3 Flash), same prompt template, temperature 0, max 4,096 output tokens
dataset_metric: ReposVul (509 vulns, C/C++/Python; vulnerable-only, so accuracy = recall); accuracy/F1. Table 6 N differs by arm (e.g., GPT-4.1 Mini C: CO N=356, CC N=204); paired McNemar is run on the overlapping subsets.
budget_control: not controlled; only the output is capped (4,096 tokens). The context arms are longer: C mean input 2,367 (CO) vs 4,785 (CC, "+102%") vs 4,586 (CK, "+94%") tokens.
arm_b: Target function plus its callee code (CC) or caller code (CK)
other_changes: none in the pipeline. The sample sets differ by arm in Table 6 because call-graph availability varies; paired tests address this.
rationale: The context block is the only manipulated prompt element, but "Adding interprocedural context nearly doubles prompt length in C" ("+102%"), and no input budget is fixed, so context type is confounded with context amount. The quoted Table 6 deltas also compare unequal-N subsets (356 vs 204); the matched comparison is the paired McNemar analysis, whose per-model C results are in the supplementary material.

comparison: Sec 5.2, Table 6: AST+PDG vs raw source, curated accuracy (ten representation variants)
model_config: qwen3.6-plus, T=0.2, max response 2,048 tokens, one query per testcase-variant; "held constant across all variants"
dataset_metric: PrimeVul-derived corpus, 107 testcases (101 retained); curated accuracy
budget_control: Explicit cap of 50,000 characters for every prompt ("The benchmark enforces a fixed maximum prompt size of 50,000 characters"). The structured arm is shorter: AST+PDG averages 7,980 input tokens vs 10,767 for raw source.
other_changes: none reported. 150/1,068 prompts were proxy_reconstructed; the authors report this moves family averages by at most 3.0%.
delta: 83.2% vs 53.5% curated accuracy (+29.7 pp); 84 vs 54 correct of 101 retained
rationale: Model, temperature, and response length are fixed "to prevent model-side confounding," and a 50,000-character cap applies to every prompt. The AST+PDG arm "uses only 7,980 input tokens on average" vs "10,767 input tokens" for raw source, so the structured arm is not longer. The cap is a ceiling, not an equalized length; 43.9% of source-only prompts were clipped.

comparison: Table 3 node ablation: full CLEAR vs No VCKG (Agent Only), and vs No Fix Intent, on PrimeVul
model_config: gpt-4o-mini, temperature 0.0, for "baselines and ablation variants"; same multi-agent architecture
budget_control: not reported for the ablation (Top-k=5 and 2-hop windowing are mentioned only for retrieval and graph construction)
arm_a: Full CLEAR: the Collector Agent retrieves Top-5 similar historical nodes from the VCKG (built from the training split), expands them along graph edges, and LLM-filters them; the Claim and other agents use these contexts
arm_b: No VCKG (Agent Only): the multi-agent pipeline without the knowledge graph. The paper does not describe what agents receive instead.
other_changes: Removing the VCKG removes the Collector's similarity-retrieval stage, graph expansion, and LLM filtering/retry step, a retrieval component and not just the shown context. Node-type ablations change what retrieval can return.
delta: P-C 19.17 (full) vs 8.08 (No VCKG) vs 14.32 (No Fix Intent); absolute P-C
rationale: The VCKG enters through a retrieval stage in which the Collector "interacts with the global VCKG to perform a semantic similarity comparison, retrieving the Top-5 most similar historical EP nodes," followed by graph expansion and LLM filtering. No VCKG removes that stage, and the paper does not say what replaces it. Context length is not reported for any arm, so even the node-type ablations are not R-strict.
